description: We are a team of computer science and engineering students interested in AI, data science, and software development. For the Field Shift challenge, we aim to build a data-driven decision-support tool that combines NASA Earth observation data with local agricultural information to help farmers explore crop rotation strategies, adapt to changing climate conditions, and improve soil and water management.
summary:
Field Shift is a bilingual English and Arabic web app that turns NASA climate data into three-year crop-rotation plans for a specific field. A farmer draws their field on a satellite map, answers a few questions (irrigation, crops of the last three years, what the farm produces for, crops they cannot grow) and balances four priorities: water, soil health, yield and climate resilience.

The backend combines long-term monthly climate normals from the NASA POWER API with ISRIC SoilGrids soil data and FAO GAEZ v5 yield references. It screens 37 crops against the field’s rainfall and temperature, tests every possible three-year sequence against crop-rotation rules, and ranks up to three distinct plans, each showing the rules, data sources and limitations behind its score. Farmers can swap a crop and see the score change before adopting a plan.

Choosing the wrong rotation can drain water, soil and income for years. Field Shift makes NASA data usable for that decision, while being clear about what the data cannot tell.
details:
What it does
Field Shift recommends three-year crop rotations for one specific field. It combines NASA climate data, global soil and yield data, and the farmer’s own answers, and explains every recommendation.

How it works

  1. The farmer draws the field on a satellite map; the backend checks the outline and computes its area in hectares.
  2. The farmer describes irrigation (source, method, reliability), crops of the last three years, farm purposes and crops they cannot grow, then sets four linked priority sliders (water, soil, yield, climate resilience) that always total 100%.
  3. An analysis runs six visible stages: field check; NASA POWER monthly temperature, rainfall and humidity normals at the field’s center; SoilGrids pH, organic carbon, nitrogen and texture across the field; screening of 37 crops (a crop is excluded only if the farmer banned it or if a rain-fed field gets less rain than the crop’s minimum; temperature and pH lower its score); FAO GAEZ v5 attainable-yield references; rotation generation.
  4. The engine takes the 14 most suitable crops, tests every three-year combination, and rejects plans that repeat a crop, use one crop family in more than two of three years, or include more than one fallow year.
  5. Each plan is scored on water fit, soil health (family diversity, legume bonus, breaking cereal runs), yield and climate fit, weighted by the farmer’s priorities. If a score has no data, its weight is shared among the others instead of counting as zero.
  6. The top three plans with different crops are shown with their rule IDs, data sources, warnings and main limitation, in English and Arabic. The farmer can swap any year’s crop, compare before and after, adopt a plan and track it on a timeline.

Benefits
Rotations that fit the field’s climate and water supply; built-in crop diversity and legume phases for soil health; transparent reasons instead of a black box; no account or password needed.

Intended impact
Give smallholder farmers, including Arabic speakers, access to decision support built on NASA data, and encourage rotations that save water and break the pest and soil-depletion cycles caused by planting the same crop family year after year.

Creativity
Priority sliders that work as a 100% budget, with weights redistributed when data is missing; every score traced to rule IDs and data sources; a sandbox to swap crops and see the effect; a full Arabic right-to-left interface; private access without passwords through a hashed browser key.

Factors we considered
The coarse resolution of global datasets (one NASA POWER point, about 0.5° grid, long-term averages, not forecasts); crop data still awaiting agronomic review, labelled as such; no global planting calendar, so temperature gives warnings rather than exclusions; graceful handling of service failures (cached or partial results); no profit or market claims; privacy.

Tools and languages
Python (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, Shapely, pyproj, rasterio, httpx); TypeScript (React 18, Vite, Tailwind, Leaflet with Geoman, TanStack Query, i18next). 73 automated tests pass (60 backend, 13 frontend). No hardware.

Use of AI
We used Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic) to help write code and documentation. The team reviewed, tested and integrated all of it.
